analysis.one_liner: Fully repeals the Affordable Care Act, ending its coverage expansions and protections starting in 2023.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in nine committees from May 2019 until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe the Affordable Care Act off the books entirely, along with the health care pieces of the 2010 follow-up law, effective January 1, 2023 [S2][S3]. That would end the insurance marketplaces and subsidies, the protections for people with preexisting conditions, the Medicaid expansion, and the taxes that paid for those programs, restoring the health care system as it existed before 2010 [S2]. It was introduced by a single member with no cosponsors and was referred to nine House committees, where nothing further happened [S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main gainers would be higher-income taxpayers (the ACA's taxes fall mostly on them and on certain industries), health insurers freed from the ACA's rules on how they must spend premium dollars, and industries like medical device makers whose ACA taxes would disappear [S2]. People who buy unsubsidized insurance and prefer fewer coverage rules would also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and the health care provisions of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, effective January 1, 2023, restoring the law as it stood before those acts [S2][S3].

Repealing the ACA would eliminate the taxes that financed it, which fall on high-income households (Medicare payroll surtax, net investment income tax) and on industries such as medical device makers and tanning services [S2].
The bill also directs that its budgetary effects be kept off the statutory PAYGO scorecards, meaning it would not trigger automatic spending cuts under those rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tens of millions of people would lose coverage or protections: the marketplace subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, guaranteed issue for preexisting conditions, dependent coverage to age 26, the ban on annual and lifetime limits, and no-cost preventive care would all end, and the ACA's Medicare drug-closure and free preventive services would be restored to pre-2010 terms [S2]. The federal deficit would rise once the ACA's taxes were removed without its spending being offset.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with preexisting conditions and subsidy recipients

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the ACA and the health provisions of the 2010 reconciliation act with no replacement, which would end marketplace subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, and protections for people with preexisting conditions on January 1, 2023 [S2][S3]. Repeal of this kind is generally estimated to leave millions more uninsured.

The bill repeals the ACA's revenue provisions along with its spending programs without offsetting either, and exempts its own budgetary effects from statutory PAYGO scorecards [S3], a combination that would substantially increase federal deficits.
A full repeal effective in one date, without a transition, would leave states, insurers, and patients with no runway to rebuild an insurance system to replace the ACA's structure [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains here go narrowly to higher-income taxpayers and to industries relieved of ACA taxes, while the costs — losing subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and preexisting-condition protections — fall broadly on ordinary people. There is no replacement plan in the bill and no transition period, so the drawbacks are severe and the benefits are concentrated.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to nine House committees (one portion went to a health subcommittee), and none of them ever took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Flores introduced the bill on May 7, 2019; it was referred that day to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and eight other committees [S1][S5].

On May 8, 2019, a portion was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and on May 21, 2019, another portion to the Subcommittee for Indigenous Peoples of the United States; neither action advanced the bill [S5].
The bill had zero cosponsors [S4], and no committee reported it, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without any further action [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who rely on ACA marketplace subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and preexisting-condition protections are better off, because the repeal never advanced; the losing side is the bill's sponsor and the higher-income taxpayers and affected industries that would have benefited from repealing the ACA's taxes.

for.name: Rep. Bill Flores
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to fully repeal the ACA and the health care provisions of the 2010 reconciliation act, effective January 1, 2023.

against.name: House committees of jurisdiction (led by Energy and Commerce)
against.role: Nine committees to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittees but never held a markup or reported it, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member sponsored the bill and no one cosponsored or voted on it, so the partisan shape of any actual support or opposition never appears in the record.

industries.note: Repeal would free insurers from ACA rules such as the medical loss ratio, guaranteed issue, and essential benefits requirements, but would also end the marketplace subsidies and mandate that steer millions of subsidized customers to them. The industry's interest ran against keeping the ACA, whose rules it paid a price to operate under.

The ACA's taxes, including the Medicare payroll surtax and the net investment income tax, fall on high earners; repeal would eliminate them, with the lost revenue meaning lost public coverage instead.

industries.industry: Medical device and other ACA-taxed industries
industries.note: Repeal would restore the law to before the ACA, eliminating the medical device excise tax and similar industry-specific taxes.
